Neonatal Yellow baboons weigh approximately 854 grams [Wwb = approximately 854 grams] at birth, a modest mass for a cercopithecine primate that reflects the relatively altricial condition of newborns in this genus. The gestation period, measured under captive conditions at a core body temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C], is 178 days [tg = 178 days], with the documented range extending from 175 to 181 days, a duration typical of large-bodied savanna primates. This intrauterine developmental period is followed by an extended phase of lactation during which the dependent suckling juvenile relies entirely on maternal milk for its nutritional needs. The transition to nutritional independence occurs at weaning, a milestone that field studies have placed at 365 days since birth [tx = 365 days since birth] at the same core temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C], signaling a gradual dietary shift toward solid foods that accelerates as the infant matures. At this point, the weaned young animal weighs about 11000 grams [Wwx = about 11000 grams], having more than doubled its birth mass during the first year of life.

Sexual maturation in male Yellow baboons is a protracted process, with puberty occurring at approximately 2007.5 days since birth [tp = approximately 2007.5 days since birth] under the typical thermoregulatory setpoint of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C], a delay that reflects the substantial somatic growth required before reproductive function can commence. At full adulthood, males attain a maximum wet body weight of 23000 grams [Wwi = 23000 grams], far exceeding the female asymptotic mass of 12000 grams [Wwi = 12000 grams], a pronounced sexual dimorphism characteristic of polygynous primate societies where male-male competition for access to females is intense. In contrast, females reach their ultimate body size earlier, having channeled energy toward growth rather than the prolonged physical development seen in males. The onset of reproductive activity in both sexes is contingent upon achieving this somatic maturity, after which individuals can engage in the complex social and physiological processes that underpin breeding success in this species.

Under captive conditions, the maximum reproductive rate for female Yellow baboons has been documented as a single infant per year [Ri = single infant per year], with a single parturition event occurring annually [F_R_i = single parturition event occurring annually] when maintained at a body temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C]. This relatively slow reproductive output is typical of large-bodied primates that invest heavily in each offspring through prolonged gestation, intensive lactation, and extended maternal care. The interbirth interval, which can range from 12 to 24 months depending on resource availability and infant survival, further constrains the lifetime reproductive success of females. In wild populations, nutritional stress and social competition can delay the resumption of cycling after parturition, reducing the effective annual birth rate below the physiological maximum observed in well-fed captive animals. This annual rate of one offspring per female is consistent with the slow life-history pace expected for a savanna-dwelling primate of this body size.

Field-based respirometry studies have established that the resting metabolic rate of adult Yellow baboons, measured at a core body temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C], is approximately 7950 milliliters per hour [JOi = approximately 7950 milliliters per hour], a value scaled to a mean body mass of 14350 grams, which represents the typical adult weight of individuals from populations where both sexes are averaged. This relatively high oxygen consumption rate reflects the energetic demands of maintaining a large brain mass, a complex digestive system optimized for omnivorous foraging, and the constant thermoregulatory costs imposed by the hot, arid savanna environment. Comparative analyses among cercopithecine primates indicate that this metabolic rate is consistent with allometric predictions based on body size, although it sits at the upper end of the expected range due to the species' active, terrestrial lifestyle. Elevated metabolic rates are likely linked to the energetic costs of daily travel distances that can exceed 10 kilometers in search of dispersed food patches, particularly during dry-season resource bottlenecks.

The lifespan of Yellow baboons in natural populations, estimated at 10950 days [am = 10950 days] under the typical body temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C], reveals a life-history strategy characterized by extended juvenile development, delayed reproduction, and prolonged post-reproductive survival in some females. This maximum longevity of approximately 30 years places the species among the longer-lived cercopithecines, a trait that is strongly associated with the species' large relative brain size and complex social structure, where older individuals serve as repositories of ecological and social knowledge for the troop. In captivity, individuals may surpass this age, with some documented cases exceeding 35 years under optimal veterinary care. The trade-off between this extended lifespan and the low annual reproductive output described earlier implies a strong reliance on high juvenile survival and stable social networks to maintain population viability, especially in fragmented habitats where anthropogenic pressures are mounting. Comparative studies with other Papio species suggest that baboons exhibit a fast-slow continuum in life-history traits.
